newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Left casts cloud over France Telecom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Left casts cloud over France Telecom.

text.p: The unexpectedly strong performance of left-wing parties in the French parliamentary election has cast a cloud over the country's biggest privatisation -- the sale of a minority stake in France Telecom.
Market sources said on Monday they would expect a left-wing government to postpone the sale, but not cancel it.
Under the original timetable, the government would have announced the price of the share sale on Monday evening.
"People have become jitterish because the outcome of the first round was not in line with expectations," said the head trader at a German bank in Paris.
"But personally, I think a left-wing government would postpone the deal and not cancel it." He said the share sale could be delayed into September, after the summer holidays.
While the Socialist Party is edging towards backing the sale of a partial stake in France Telecom following comments it would not privatise the operator, the Communist Party remains hostile.
Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin said last week he would first consult France Telecom staff before taking a firm decision on whether to sell shares or not.
By coincidence, the sale of a 30 to 35 percent stake in France Telecom was originally due to enter its final lap on Monday with the announcement of the sale price.
While private investors would have had since May 6 to subscribe to shares, the Initial Public Offering (IPO) would have started on Tuesday and last until June 3.
The centre-right government decided on April 22 to postpone the operation by four weeks. This was one day after President Jacques Chirac called the snap election.

At the time, financial analysts estimated the value of France Telecom at between 160 billion francs ($28.1 billion) and 210 billion francs which would have made it relatively easy for the state to raise the 30 to 50 billion francs it sought.

The proceeds from the sale cannot be used to cut the budget deficit but go towards the national debt. However, privatisation revenues can be used to offset capital injections in other state companies.

Any French government will need money in 1997 to help bank Credit Lyonnais, insurance group GAN -- Ste Centrale du Groupe des Assurances Nationales -- the SFP film studios, Thomson Multimedia and artillery and battle tank maker GIAT Industrie.

At the time Chirac called the election, the CAC-40 index of French blue-chip shares stood at 2,522.67. By May 16 it had risen to an all-time high of 2,804.51, but plunged more than three percent to around 2,676.50 on Monday following Sunday's first round of the polls.
These changes in the French share prices indicate that the France Telecom sale could have taken place at a higher price than the range of 170 to 180 francs per share seen early April.
Even after Monday's sharp fall, the overall market price level was still six percent above that in April.

The unexpected gains for the left wing -- obtaining a 4.5 percentage point lead over the ruling centre-right parties in the first round of the election -- pulled down a number of other privatisation-related shares.
Dassault Aviation, set to merge with state-owned Aerospatiale, was suspended limit down at the opening at its lower limit of 1,112 francs, compared with its Friday close of 1,230.
Thomson-CSF, the defence electronics company in which the state plans to sell a 58-percent stake, dropped 8.6 percent to 173.2 francs.
Thomson bidders Lagardere Groupe fell 5.18 percent to 175.7 francs, and Alcatel Alsthom 3.53 percent to 656 francs. At 1240 GMT, the CAC-40 blue-chip index was down 3.72 percent.
"Such a reaction is normal," said one trader about the privatisation stocks. "There is suddenly a new uncertainty and markets hate uncertainty." ($ = 5.690 French Francs)
